nodes.name: Ring of integer matrices $M_n(\mathbb{Z})$
nodes.statement: For a positive integer $n$, let $M_n(\mathbb{Z})$ denote the ring of $n\times n$ integer matrices.

nodes.name: Symmetric matrix
nodes.statement: A matrix $A\in M_n(\mathbb{Z})$ is called \emph{symmetric} if $A^T = A$.

nodes.name: Congruence preserves symmetry
nodes.statement: If $A$ is symmetric and $U\in M_n(\mathbb{Z})$ is any matrix, then \[ (U^T A U)^T = U^T A^T (U^T)^T = U^T A U, \] so $U^T A U$ is again symmetric.
conclusions: $U^T A U$ is again symmetric
nodes.statement_short: If $A$ is symmetric then $U^TAU$ is symmetric for any integer matrix $U$.

nodes.name: Special linear group $\mathrm{SL}_n(\mathbb{Z})$
nodes.statement: Let $\mathrm{SL}_n(\mathbb{Z})$ denote the group of $n\times n$ integer matrices of determinant $1$.

nodes.name: Action of $\mathrm{SL}_n(\mathbb{Z})$ on $M_n(\mathbb{Z})$
nodes.statement: This group acts on $M_n(\mathbb{Z})$ by \[ A \cdot U := U^T A U \qquad (A\in M_n(\mathbb{Z}),\ U\in \mathrm{SL}_n(\mathbb{Z})). \] Indeed, \[A \cdot (UV) = (UV)^T A (UV) = V^T(U^T A U)V = (A\cdot U)\cdot V, \] and $A\cdot I = A$, so this is a right group action.
nodes.statement_short: $\mathrm{SL}_n(\mathbb{Z})$ (determinant-1 integer matrices) acts on the right on $M_n(\mathbb{Z})$ by $A\cdot U = U^TAU$.

nodes.name: Equivalence of integer matrices
nodes.statement: Two matrices $A,B\in M_n(\mathbb{Z})$ are \emph{equivalent}, and we write $A\sim B$, if there exists $U\in\mathrm{SL}_n(\mathbb{Z})$ such that \[ B = A\cdot U = U^T A U. \] It is easy to check that $\sim$ is an equivalence relation.
differentia: there exists $U\in\mathrm{SL}_n(\mathbb{Z})$ such that \[ B = A\cdot U = U^T A U. \]
nodes.statement_short: $A\sim B$ iff $B=U^TAU$ for some $U\in\mathrm{SL}_n(\mathbb{Z})$; an equivalence relation.

nodes.name: Equivalence preserves determinant
nodes.statement: This equivalence relation preserves determinants, that is, if $A\sim B$, then $\det(A) = \det(B)$.
conclusions: $\det(A) = \det(B)$
nodes.label: lem:mat_det_preserved

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 1
nodes.statement: Since $\det U = 1$ for $U\in\mathrm{SL}_n(\mathbb{Z})$, we have \[ \det(A\cdot U) = \det(U^T A U) = \det(U^T)\det(A)\det(U) = \det(A),\] so the action preserves determinants.
nodes.statement_short: Multiplicativity of det with $\det U = 1$.

nodes.name: Equivalence preserves symmetry
nodes.statement: If $A\sim B$, then $A$ is symmetric if and only if $B$ is symmetric.
conclusions: $A$ is symmetric if and only if $B$ is symmetric
nodes.label: lem:mat_symm_preserved

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2
nodes.statement: Easy check both in math and in \sf{lean}.
nodes.statement_short: Asserted as an easy check.

nodes.name: Equivalence classes of symmetric matrices of fixed determinant
nodes.statement: Thus for any integer $d$, this action partitions the set of symmetric $n\times n$ matrices of determinant $d$ into equivalence classes.
nodes.statement_short: The $\mathrm{SL}_n(\mathbb{Z})$ action partitions symmetric matrices of determinant $d$ into classes.
conclusions: this action partitions the set of symmetric $n\times n$ matrices of determinant $d$ into equivalence classes

nodes.name: Quadratic form associated to a symmetric matrix
nodes.statement: The \emph{quadratic form} associated to a symmetric matrix $A=(a_{i,j})\in M_n(\mathbb{Z})$ is the map \[ F_A(x_1,\dots,x_n) = \sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^n a_{i,j} x_i x_j . \]
nodes.statement_short: $F_A(x)=\sum_{i,j} a_{i,j}x_ix_j$ for symmetric integer $A$.

nodes.name: Matrix notation $x^TAx$ for a quadratic form
nodes.statement: If we view $x$ as the column vector \[ x = \begin{pmatrix}x_1\\ \vdots\\ x_n\end{pmatrix}, \] then the quadratic form can be written concisely as \[ F_A(x_1,\dots,x_n) = x^T A x . \]
nodes.statement_short: Viewing $x$ as a column vector, $F_A(x)=x^TAx$.

nodes.name: Discriminant of a quadratic form
nodes.statement: The \emph{discriminant} of the quadratic form $F_A$ is defined to be \[ \operatorname{disc}(F_A) := \det(A). \]

nodes.name: Equivalence of quadratic forms
nodes.statement: If $A$ and $B$ are symmetric matrices and $F_A, F_B$ their associated quadratic forms, we say $F_A$ and $F_B$ are \emph{equivalent}, and write $F_A\sim F_B$, if $A\sim B$ as matrices; that is, if there exists $U\in\mathrm{SL}_n(\mathbb{Z})$ with $B = U^T A U$. Equivalence of forms is again an equivalence relation.
nodes.statement_short: Forms are equivalent iff their matrices are $\mathrm{SL}_n(\mathbb{Z})$-congruent.
nodes.label: def:QuadMap_equiv

nodes.name: Equivalent forms have the same discriminant
nodes.statement: Equivalent forms have the same discriminant.
conclusions: have the same discriminant
nodes.label: lem:QuadMap_equiv_to_det_eq

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3
nodes.statement: Trivial from Lemma~\ref{lem:mat_det_preserved}.
nodes.statement_short: Immediate from Lemma 1.

nodes.name: Representation of a natural number by a quadratic form
nodes.statement: A quadratic form $F_A$ \emph{represents} an natural number $N$ if there exist integers $x_1,\dots,x_n$ such that \[ F_A(x_1,\dots,x_n) = N. \]
differentia: there exist integers $x_1,\dots,x_n$ such that \[ F_A(x_1,\dots,x_n) = N. \]
nodes.label: def:Nat_is_represented_by

nodes.name: Value transformation under equivalence
nodes.statement: If $F_A\sim F_B$, then $B = U^T A U$ for some $U\in\mathrm{SL}_n(\mathbb{Z})$, and for any integer vector $x$ we have \[F_A(x) = F_B(U \cdot x).\]
conclusions: $B = U^T A U$ for some $U\in\mathrm{SL}_n(\mathbb{Z})$
for any integer vector $x$ we have \[F_A(x) = F_B(U \cdot x).\]
nodes.statement_short: Equivalent forms satisfy $F_A(x)=F_B(Ux)$ for the transforming matrix $U$.
nodes.label: lem:QuadMap_equiv_apply

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4
nodes.statement: By direct calculation.
nodes.statement_short: Direct calculation.

nodes.name: Equivalent forms represent the same integers
nodes.statement: Hence, if $F_A$ represents $N$, then $F_B$ also represents $N$. Therefore any two equivalent forms represent exactly the same set of integers.
conclusions: $F_B$ also represents $N$
any two equivalent forms represent exactly the same set of integers
nodes.label: lem:QuadMap_equiv_represents

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5
nodes.statement: Easy follows from ~\ref{lem:QuadMap_equiv_apply}.
nodes.statement_short: Follows from Lemma 4.

nodes.name: Forms equivalent to sum of $n\ge4$ squares represent all non-negative integers
nodes.statement: For $n\ge4$, Lagrange's four–squares theorem implies that every quadratic form equivalent to $x_1^2+\cdots+x_n^2$ represents all non–negative integers.
conclusions: every quadratic form equivalent to $x_1^2+\cdots+x_n^2$ represents all non–negative integers

nodes.name: Positive-definite quadratic form
nodes.statement: A quadratic form $F_A$ is \emph{positive–definite} if \[ F_A(x_1,\dots,x_n) > 0 \] for every non–zero vector $(x_1,\dots,x_n)\in\mathbb{Z}^n$. Any form equivalent to a positive–definite form is again positive–definite.
nodes.label: def:QuadMap_posdef

nodes.name: Positive-definiteness is invariant under equivalence
nodes.statement: If a quadratic map $P$ is positive–definite and $P\sim Q$ as quadratic maps, then $Q$ is positive–definite.
conclusions: $Q$ is positive–definite
nodes.label: lem:QuadMap_posdef_equiv

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 6
nodes.statement: Trivial follows from the definiton of positive-definite.
nodes.statement_short: Immediate from the definition of positive-definite.

nodes.name: Binary and ternary quadratic forms
nodes.statement: A quadratic form in two variables is called a \emph{binary} quadratic form; a quadratic form in three variables is called a \emph{ternary} quadratic form.

nodes.name: Binary quadratic form $F_A(x_1,x_2)$ of a $2\times2$ symmetric matrix
nodes.statement: Let \[ A = \begin{pmatrix} a_{1,1} & a_{1,2}\\[0.3em] a_{1,2} & a_{2,2} \end{pmatrix} \] be a symmetric $2\times2$ matrix with integer entries, and let \[ F_A(x_1,x_2) = a_{1,1}x_1^2 + 2a_{1,2}x_1x_2 + a_{2,2}x_2^2 \] be the associated binary quadratic form.
nodes.statement_short: Notation: $A$ symmetric $2\times2$ with entries $a_{i,j}$ and $F_A=a_{1,1}x_1^2+2a_{1,2}x_1x_2+a_{2,2}x_2^2$.

nodes.name: Discriminant $d$ of a binary form
nodes.statement: The discriminant of $F_A$ is \[ d = \det(A) = a_{1,1}a_{2,2} - a_{1,2}^2. \]

nodes.name: Discriminant is just the determinant; Mathlib's quadratic maps
nodes.statement: Although we "defined" the discriminant of a quadratic form, since it really is just the determinant of the associate matrix (and in the reference whenever we talk about properties about quadratic we almost always mean the properties about the underlying matrix and there will always be one since we defined it that way). Note that in mathlib there is a different definition of a quadratic map which doesn't involve matrix.
nodes.statement_short: The discriminant is only the determinant of the matrix; Mathlib defines quadratic maps without matrices.

nodes.name: Positive-definiteness criterion for binary forms
nodes.statement: The binary quadratic form $F_A$ is positive–definite if and only if \[ a_{1,1} > 0 \quad\text{and}\quad d = a_{1,1}a_{2,2}-a_{1,2}^2 > 0. \]
conclusions: The binary quadratic form $F_A$ is positive–definite if and only if \[ a_{1,1} > 0 \quad\text{and}\quad d = a_{1,1}a_{2,2}-a_{1,2}^2 > 0. \]
equivalent_conditions: The binary quadratic form $F_A$ is positive–definite
nodes.statement_short: A binary form is positive definite iff $a_{1,1}>0$ and $d>0$.
nodes.label: lem:binary_posdef

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 7
nodes.statement: First suppose $F_A$ is positive–definite. Then \[ F_A(1,0) = a_{1,1} > 0. \] Next consider the vector $(-a_{1,2},a_{1,1})$; since it is not zero, positive–definiteness implies \[ 0 < F_A(-a_{1,2},a_{1,1}) = a_{1,1}a_{1,2}^2 - 2a_{1,2}^2 a_{1,1} + a_{1,1}^2 a_{2,2} = a_{1,1}(a_{1,1}a_{2,2}-a_{1,2}^2) = a_{1,1}d. \] Since $a_{1,1}>0$, it follows that $d>0$. Conversely, assume $a_{1,1}>0$ and $d>0$. We rewrite the form by completing the square: \[ a_{1,1} F_A(x_1,x_2) = (a_{1,1}x_1 + a_{1,2}x_2)^2 + d\,x_2^2. \] The right-hand side is a sum of two non–negative terms, and it is zero if and only if \[ a_{1,1}x_1 + a_{1,2}x_2 = 0 \quad\text{and}\quad x_2 = 0. \] From $x_2=0$ we get $x_1=0$, so the only zero of $F_A$ is $(0,0)$. Hence $F_A$ is positive–definite.
nodes.statement_short: Evaluate at $(1,0)$ and $(-a_{1,2},a_{1,1})$ for necessity; complete the square for sufficiency.

nodes.name: Necessity
nodes.statement: First suppose $F_A$ is positive–definite. Then \[ F_A(1,0) = a_{1,1} > 0. \] Next consider the vector $(-a_{1,2},a_{1,1})$; since it is not zero, positive–definiteness implies \[ 0 < F_A(-a_{1,2},a_{1,1}) = a_{1,1}a_{1,2}^2 - 2a_{1,2}^2 a_{1,1} + a_{1,1}^2 a_{2,2} = a_{1,1}(a_{1,1}a_{2,2}-a_{1,2}^2) = a_{1,1}d. \] Since $a_{1,1}>0$, it follows that $d>0$.
nodes.statement_short: Positive-definite implies $a_{1,1}>0$ and $a_{1,1}d>0$.

nodes.name: Sufficiency
nodes.statement: Conversely, assume $a_{1,1}>0$ and $d>0$. We rewrite the form by completing the square: \[ a_{1,1} F_A(x_1,x_2) = (a_{1,1}x_1 + a_{1,2}x_2)^2 + d\,x_2^2. \] The right-hand side is a sum of two non–negative terms, and it is zero if and only if \[ a_{1,1}x_1 + a_{1,2}x_2 = 0 \quad\text{and}\quad x_2 = 0. \] From $x_2=0$ we get $x_1=0$, so the only zero of $F_A$ is $(0,0)$. Hence $F_A$ is positive–definite.
nodes.statement_short: Complete the square: $a_{1,1}F_A=(a_{1,1}x_1+a_{1,2}x_2)^2+dx_2^2$ vanishes only at 0.

nodes.name: Reduction of positive-definite binary forms
nodes.statement: Let $d>0$. Every equivalence class of positive–definite binary quadratic forms of discriminant $d$ contains a form \[ F_A(x_1,x_2) = a_{1,1}x_1^2 + 2a_{1,2}x_1x_2 + a_{2,2}x_2^2 \] such that \[ 2|a_{1,2}| \le a_{1,1} \le a_{2,2} \qquad\text{and}\qquad a_{1,1}^2 \le \frac{4}{3}d. \]
conclusions: Every equivalence class of positive–definite binary quadratic forms of discriminant $d$ contains a form \[ F_A(x_1,x_2) = a_{1,1}x_1^2 + 2a_{1,2}x_1x_2 + a_{2,2}x_2^2 \] such that \[ 2|a_{1,2}| \le a_{1,1} \le a_{2,2} \qquad\text{and}\qquad a_{1,1}^2 \le \frac{4}{3}d. \]
nodes.statement_short: Each class of positive-definite binary forms of discriminant $d$ has a reduced form with $2|a_{1,2}|\le a_{1,1}\le a_{2,2}$, $a_{1,1}^2\le 4d/3$.
nodes.label: lem:binary-reduction

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 8
nodes.statement:
Let $F$ be a positive–definite binary quadratic form of discriminant $d$, and let $C$ be the corresponding symmetric matrix. Among all forms equivalent to $F$, choose one whose associated matrix $B = (b_{i,j})$ represents the smallest positive integer; that is, let $a_{1,1}$ be the least positive value taken by $F$, and choose an integer vector $(u_1,u_2)$ with \[ F(u_1,u_2) = a_{1,1}. \] By applying a suitable unimodular change of variables we may assume $(u_1,u_2) = (1,0)$, so that in this basis the matrix has the form \[ B =  egin{pmatrix} a_{1,1} & b_{1,2}\[0.3em] b_{1,2} & b_{2,2} \end{pmatrix}, \] and $F_B(1,0) = a_{1,1}$ is the smallest positive integer represented by any form equivalent to $F$. 
oindent \emph{Step 1: Making $|b_{1,2}|$ small.}\ Consider the unimodular matrix \[ U_t =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & t\[0.3em] 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \in \mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{Z}) \qquad (t\in\mathbb{Z}). \] Replacing $B$ by \[ A_t := U_t^T B U_t \] does not change the equivalence class. A straightforward calculation shows that the new coefficients are \[ a_{1,1} = b_{1,1},\qquad a_{1,2} = b_{1,2} + a_{1,1} t,\qquad a_{2,2} = F_B(t,1). \] As $t$ varies over $\mathbb{Z}$, the numbers $a_{1,2}$ run through an entire congruence class modulo $a_{1,1}$. Hence we may choose $t$ so that \[ |a_{1,2}| \le  rac{a_{1,1}}{2}, \] which is equivalent to $2|a_{1,2}|\le a_{1,1}$. 
oindent \emph{Step 2: Ensuring $a_{1,1}\le a_{2,2}$.}\ If $a_{2,2}<a_{1,1}$ for the matrix $A_t$, we can apply the symmetry of the variables and replace $(x_1,x_2)$ by $(x_2,x_1)$. Algebraically, this corresponds to conjugating by the permutation matrix \[ P =  egin{pmatrix}0&1\ 1&0\end{pmatrix}\in\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{Z}), \] which interchanges $a_{1,1}$ and $a_{2,2}$ but leaves the discriminant and the property $2|a_{1,2}|\le a_{1,1}$ unchanged. After at most one such step we obtain a matrix $A$ satisfying \[ 2|a_{1,2}|\le a_{1,1}\le a_{2,2}. \] 
oindent \emph{Step 3: Bounding $a_{1,1}$ in terms of $d$.}\ For this reduced matrix $A$ we have \[ d = \det(A) = a_{1,1}a_{2,2} - a_{1,2}^2. \] Using $a_{2,2}\ge a_{1,1}$ and $|a_{1,2}|\le a_{1,1}/2$, we obtain \[ d \ge a_{1,1}^2 - \Bigl( rac{a_{1,1}}{2}\Bigr)^2 = a_{1,1}^2 -  rac{a_{1,1}^2}{4} =  rac{3}{4} a_{1,1}^2. \] Hence \[ a_{1,1}^2 \le  rac{4}{3} d. \] Thus we have found, in the equivalence class of $F$, a form with the desired properties.
nodes.statement_short: Take a form in the class minimizing the represented value $a_{1,1}$, then shear and swap variables. The bound follows from $d\ge a_{1,1}^2-a_{1,1}^2/4$.

nodes.name: Choose minimal representative
nodes.statement: Let $F$ be a positive–definite binary quadratic form of discriminant $d$, and let $C$ be the corresponding symmetric matrix. Among all forms equivalent to $F$, choose one whose associated matrix $B = (b_{i,j})$ represents the smallest positive integer; that is, let $a_{1,1}$ be the least positive value taken by $F$, and choose an integer vector $(u_1,u_2)$ with \[ F(u_1,u_2) = a_{1,1}. \] By applying a suitable unimodular change of variables we may assume $(u_1,u_2) = (1,0)$, so that in this basis the matrix has the form \[ B = \begin{pmatrix} a_{1,1} & b_{1,2}\\[0.3em] b_{1,2} & b_{2,2} \end{pmatrix}, \] and $F_B(1,0) = a_{1,1}$ is the smallest positive integer represented by any form equivalent to $F$.
nodes.statement_short: Choose an equivalent form whose $(1,1)$ entry is the least positive value of $F$.

nodes.name: Step 1: making $|b_{1,2}|$ small
nodes.statement: \emph{Step 1: Making $|b_{1,2}|$ small.}\\ Consider the unimodular matrix \[ U_t = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & t\\[0.3em] 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \in \mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{Z}) \qquad (t\in\mathbb{Z}). \] Replacing $B$ by \[ A_t := U_t^T B U_t \] does not change the equivalence class. A straightforward calculation shows that the new coefficients are \[ a_{1,1} = b_{1,1},\qquad a_{1,2} = b_{1,2} + a_{1,1} t,\qquad a_{2,2} = F_B(t,1). \] As $t$ varies over $\mathbb{Z}$, the numbers $a_{1,2}$ run through an entire congruence class modulo $a_{1,1}$. Hence we may choose $t$ so that \[ |a_{1,2}| \le \frac{a_{1,1}}{2}, \] which is equivalent to $2|a_{1,2}|\le a_{1,1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Shear by $U_t$ to get $|a_{1,2}|\le a_{1,1}/2$.

nodes.name: Step 2: ensuring $a_{1,1}\le a_{2,2}$
nodes.statement: \emph{Step 2: Ensuring $a_{1,1}\le a_{2,2}$.}\\ If $a_{2,2}<a_{1,1}$ for the matrix $A_t$, we can apply the symmetry of the variables and replace $(x_1,x_2)$ by $(x_2,x_1)$. Algebraically, this corresponds to conjugating by the permutation matrix \[ P = \begin{pmatrix}0&1\\ 1&0\end{pmatrix}\in\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{Z}), \] which interchanges $a_{1,1}$ and $a_{2,2}$ but leaves the discriminant and the property $2|a_{1,2}|\le a_{1,1}$ unchanged. After at most one such step we obtain a matrix $A$ satisfying \[ 2|a_{1,2}|\le a_{1,1}\le a_{2,2}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Swap variables if needed so that $a_{1,1}\le a_{2,2}$.

nodes.name: Step 3: bounding $a_{1,1}$
nodes.statement: \emph{Step 3: Bounding $a_{1,1}$ in terms of $d$.}\\ For this reduced matrix $A$ we have \[ d = \det(A) = a_{1,1}a_{2,2} - a_{1,2}^2. \] Using $a_{2,2}\ge a_{1,1}$ and $|a_{1,2}|\le a_{1,1}/2$, we obtain \[ d \ge a_{1,1}^2 - \Bigl(\frac{a_{1,1}}{2}\Bigr)^2 = a_{1,1}^2 - \frac{a_{1,1}^2}{4} = \frac{3}{4} a_{1,1}^2. \] Hence \[ a_{1,1}^2 \le \frac{4}{3} d. \] Thus we have found, in the equivalence class of $F$, a form with the desired properties.

nodes.name: Positive-definite binary forms of discriminant 1
nodes.statement: Every positive–definite binary quadratic form of discriminant $1$ is equivalent to the form \[ x_1^2 + x_2^2. \]
assumptions: positive–definite binary quadratic form of discriminant $1$
conclusions: is equivalent to the form \[ x_1^2 + x_2^2. \]
nodes.statement_short: Every positive-definite binary form of discriminant 1 is equivalent to $x_1^2+x_2^2$.
nodes.label: thm:binary_quadMap_det_eq_one

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1
nodes.statement: Let $F$ be a positive–definite binary quadratic form of discriminant $d=1$, and let $F_A$ be a reduced representative as in Lemma~\ref{lem:binary-reduction}. Thus \[ F_A(x_1,x_2) = a_{1,1}x_1^2 + 2a_{1,2}x_1x_2 + a_{2,2}x_2^2, \] with \[ 2|a_{1,2}|\le a_{1,1}\le a_{2,2} \qquad\text{and}\qquad a_{1,1}^2 \le \frac{4}{3}d = \frac{4}{3}. \] Since $a_{1,1}$ is a positive integer, the inequality $a_{1,1}^2 \le 4/3$ forces $a_{1,1}=1$. Then $2|a_{1,2}|\le a_{1,1}=1$ implies $a_{1,2}=0$. Finally, the discriminant condition \[ 1 = d = a_{1,1}a_{2,2}-a_{1,2}^2 = 1\cdot a_{2,2}-0 \] gives $a_{2,2}=1$. Thus $A$ is the identity matrix, and the corresponding form is \[ F_A(x_1,x_2) = x_1^2 + x_2^2. \] Therefore $F$ is equivalent to $x_1^2 + x_2^2$, which completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the reduction lemma with $d=1$; the bounds force $A=I$.

nodes.name: Take a reduced representative
nodes.statement: Let $F$ be a positive–definite binary quadratic form of discriminant $d=1$, and let $F_A$ be a reduced representative as in Lemma~\ref{lem:binary-reduction}. Thus \[ F_A(x_1,x_2) = a_{1,1}x_1^2 + 2a_{1,2}x_1x_2 + a_{2,2}x_2^2, \] with \[ 2|a_{1,2}|\le a_{1,1}\le a_{2,2} \qquad\text{and}\qquad a_{1,1}^2 \le \frac{4}{3}d = \frac{4}{3}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Pick a reduced representative via Lemma 8.

nodes.name: Force identity matrix
nodes.statement: Since $a_{1,1}$ is a positive integer, the inequality $a_{1,1}^2 \le 4/3$ forces $a_{1,1}=1$. Then $2|a_{1,2}|\le a_{1,1}=1$ implies $a_{1,2}=0$. Finally, the discriminant condition \[ 1 = d = a_{1,1}a_{2,2}-a_{1,2}^2 = 1\cdot a_{2,2}-0 \] gives $a_{2,2}=1$. Thus $A$ is the identity matrix, and the corresponding form is \[ F_A(x_1,x_2) = x_1^2 + x_2^2. \] Therefore $F$ is equivalent to $x_1^2 + x_2^2$, which completes the proof.

nodes.name: Binary form $G_A$ attached to a ternary form
nodes.statement: Let $A = (a_{i,j})$ be a $3\times 3$ symmetric matrix with integer entries, and let \[ F_A(x_1,x_2,x_3) = \sum_{1 \le i,j \le 3} a_{i,j} x_i x_j \] be the associated ternary quadratic form. Define the binary quadratic form \[ G_A(x_2,x_3) \] by the identity \begin{equation} a_{1,1} F_A(x_1,x_2,x_3) = (a_{1,1} x_1 + a_{1,2} x_2 + a_{1,3} x_3)^2 + G_A(x_2,x_3). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: For a ternary form $F_A$, $G_A$ is the binary form with $a_{1,1}F_A=(a_{1,1}x_1+a_{1,2}x_2+a_{1,3}x_3)^2+G_A$.
nodes.label: def:QuadMap_Tenary_G

nodes.name: Determinant of $G_A$
nodes.statement: Let $A$ be any symmetric $3\times 3$ matrix with integer entries. Then \[det(G_A) = A_{11} * det(A)\].
assumptions: $A$ be any symmetric $3\times 3$ matrix with integer entries
nodes.label: lem:QuadMap_Tenary_G_det

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 9
nodes.statement: By direct calculation.
nodes.statement_short: Direct calculation.

nodes.name: Evaluation identity for $G_A$
nodes.statement: For any $A \in M_n(\mathbb{Z})$ where $A$ is symmetric and for any $v \in \mathbb{Z}^3$, we have that \[ A_{11} * F_A(v) = (A_{11} v_1 + A_{12}v_2 + A_{23}v_3)^2 + G_A(v_2, v_3). \]
nodes.label: lem:ternary_G_apply

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 10
nodes.statement: After unfolding all the definitions this is just a direct calculation (by construction of $G$).
nodes.statement_short: Unfold definitions; direct calculation.

nodes.name: Positive-definiteness criterion for ternary forms
nodes.statement: The ternary form $F_A$ is positive-definite if and only if the three integers \[ a_{1,1},\qquad d' = a_{1,1}a_{2,2} - a_{1,2}^2,\qquad d = \det(A) \] are all positive.
conclusions: The ternary form $F_A$ is positive-definite if and only if the three integers \[ a_{1,1},\qquad d' = a_{1,1}a_{2,2} - a_{1,2}^2,\qquad d = \det(A) \] are all positive.
equivalent_conditions: the three integers \[ a_{1,1},\qquad d' = a_{1,1}a_{2,2} - a_{1,2}^2,\qquad d = \det(A) \] are all positive
nodes.statement_short: A ternary form is positive definite iff $a_{1,1}$, $a_{1,1}a_{2,2}-a_{1,2}^2$ and $\det A$ are positive.
nodes.label: lem:ternary_posdef_iff

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 11
nodes.statement: Assume first that $F_A$ is positive-definite. Fix integers $x_2, x_3$ such that $(x_2,x_3) \neq (0,0)$, and choose \[ x_1 = -\frac{a_{1,2} x_2 + a_{1,3} x_3}{a_{1,1}}. \] Then \[ a_{1,1} F_A(x_1, x_2, x_3) = (a_{1,1}x_1 + a_{1,2}x_2 + a_{1,3}x_3)^2 + G_A(x_2,x_3) = G_A(x_2,x_3). \] Since $F_A$ is positive-definite, the left side is $>0$, so $G_A$ is a positive‐definite binary quadratic form. By Lemma ~\ref{lem:binary_posdef} this implies \[ a_{1,1} > 0,\qquad d' = a_{1,1}a_{2,2} - a_{1,2}^2 > 0. \] Also the discriminant of $G_A$ is $d > 0$, hence $\det(A) > 0$. Conversely, assume $a_{1,1}, d', d > 0$. Then $G_A$ is positive-definite (~\ref{lem:binary_posdef}). If $F_A(x_1,x_2,x_3) = 0$, then \eqref{eq:1.3} gives \[ (a_{1,1}x_1 + a_{1,2}x_2 + a_{1,3}x_3)^2 + G_A(x_2,x_3) = 0. \] Since both terms on the right are nonnegative, they must vanish. Thus $x_2 = x_3 = 0$, and then the linear term forces $x_1 = 0$. Hence $F_A$ is positive-definite.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to the binary form $G_A$ via identity (1) and apply the binary criterion in both directions.

nodes.name: Necessity
nodes.statement: Assume first that $F_A$ is positive-definite. Fix integers $x_2, x_3$ such that $(x_2,x_3) \neq (0,0)$, and choose \[ x_1 = -\frac{a_{1,2} x_2 + a_{1,3} x_3}{a_{1,1}}. \] Then \[ a_{1,1} F_A(x_1, x_2, x_3) = (a_{1,1}x_1 + a_{1,2}x_2 + a_{1,3}x_3)^2 + G_A(x_2,x_3) = G_A(x_2,x_3). \] Since $F_A$ is positive-definite, the left side is $>0$, so $G_A$ is a positive‐definite binary quadratic form. By Lemma ~\ref{lem:binary_posdef} this implies \[ a_{1,1} > 0,\qquad d' = a_{1,1}a_{2,2} - a_{1,2}^2 > 0. \] Also the discriminant of $G_A$ is $d > 0$, hence $\det(A) > 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Positive-definite $F_A$ makes $G_A$ positive-definite; apply Lemma 7.

nodes.name: Sufficiency
nodes.statement: Conversely, assume $a_{1,1}, d', d > 0$. Then $G_A$ is positive-definite (~\ref{lem:binary_posdef}). If $F_A(x_1,x_2,x_3) = 0$, then \eqref{eq:1.3} gives \[ (a_{1,1}x_1 + a_{1,2}x_2 + a_{1,3}x_3)^2 + G_A(x_2,x_3) = 0. \] Since both terms on the right are nonnegative, they must vanish. Thus $x_2 = x_3 = 0$, and then the linear term forces $x_1 = 0$. Hence $F_A$ is positive-definite.
nodes.statement_short: $G_A$ positive-definite; a zero of $F_A$ forces both squares in (1) to vanish.

nodes.name: Change of variables preserving $b_{1,1}$ and $G$
nodes.statement: Let $B = (b_{i,j})$ be a symmetric $3\times 3$ matrix such that $F_B$ is positive-definite, and let $G_B$ be the corresponding positive-definite binary quadratic form, defined by \[ b_{1,1} F_B(y_1,y_2,y_3) = (b_{1,1}y_1 + b_{1,2}y_2 + b_{1,3}y_3)^2 + G_B(y_2, y_3). \] For each $V \in SL_2(\mathbb{Z})$, define \[ A^* = (V^*)^T B V^*, \] and let $G_{A^*}$ be the binary form attached to $A^*$. For integers $r,s$, define \[ V_{r,s} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & r & s \\ 0 & v_{11} & v_{12} \\ 0 & v_{21} & v_{22} \end{pmatrix} \in SL_3(\mathbb{Z}), \qquad A_{r,s} = V_{r,s}^T B V_{r,s}. \] Then $a_{1,1} = b_{1,1}$ and \[ a_{1,1} F_{A_{r,s}}(x_1,x_2,x_3) = (a_{1,1}x_1 + a_{1,2}x_2 + a_{1,3}x_3)^2 + G_{A^*}(x_2,x_3), \] and $A^*$ is independent of $r$ and $s$.
assumptions: Let $B = (b_{i,j})$ be a symmetric $3\times 3$ matrix such that $F_B$ is positive-definite, and let $G_B$ be the corresponding positive-definite binary quadratic form, defined by \[ b_{1,1} F_B(y_1,y_2,y_3) = (b_{1,1}y_1 + b_{1,2}y_2 + b_{1,3}y_3)^2 + G_B(y_2, y_3). \]
conclusions: $A^*$ is independent of $r$ and $s$
nodes.statement_short: Transforming $B$ by the block matrix $V_{r,s}$ keeps $b_{1,1}$ and replaces $G_B$ by $G_{A^*}$, independent of $r,s$.
nodes.label: lem:ternary_lemma4

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 12
nodes.statement: A direct calculation using the block structure of $V_{r,s}$ shows that the upper‐left $1\times 1$ entry of $A_{r,s}$ equals $b_{1,1}$ and that the lower $2\times 2$ block of $A_{r,s}$ equals the matrix $A^*$. Substituting these expressions into \eqref{eq:1.3} gives the identity claimed.
nodes.statement_short: Block-matrix calculation, then substitute into (1).

nodes.name: Completing a primitive vector to an $SL_3(\mathbb{Z})$ matrix
nodes.statement: If integers $u_{1,1},u_{2,1},u_{3,1}$ satisfy \[ \gcd(u_{1,1},u_{2,1},u_{3,1}) = 1, \] then there exist integers $u_{i,j}$ for $i=1,2,3$ and $j=2,3$ such that the matrix \[ U = (u_{i,j}) \in SL_3(\mathbb{Z}). \]
conclusions: there exist integers $u_{i,j}$ for $i=1,2,3$ and $j=2,3$ such that the matrix \[ U = (u_{i,j}) \in SL_3(\mathbb{Z}). \]
nodes.statement_short: A primitive integer vector is the first column of some matrix in $SL_3(\mathbb{Z})$.

nodes.name: Proof of Construction (completion to $SL_3$)
nodes.statement: Let $\gcd(u_{1,1},u_{2,1}) = a$. Choose integers $u_{1,2},u_{2,2}$ such that \[ u_{1,1}u_{2,2} - u_{2,1}u_{1,2} = a. \] Since $\gcd(a,u_{3,1}) = 1$, choose integers $u_{3,3}, b$ such that \[ a u_{3,3} - b u_{3,1} = 1. \] Set \[ u_{1,3} = b,\qquad u_{2,3} = 0,\qquad u_{3,2} = 0. \] Then the resulting matrix $U$ has determinant $1$.
nodes.statement_short: Explicit construction via two Bezout identities.

nodes.name: Second Bezout step
nodes.statement: Since $\gcd(a,u_{3,1}) = 1$, choose integers $u_{3,3}, b$ such that \[ a u_{3,3} - b u_{3,1} = 1. \]

nodes.name: Assemble the matrix
nodes.statement: Set \[ u_{1,3} = b,\qquad u_{2,3} = 0,\qquad u_{3,2} = 0. \] Then the resulting matrix $U$ has determinant $1$.
nodes.statement_short: Fill remaining entries; the matrix has determinant 1.

nodes.name: Reduction of positive-definite ternary forms
nodes.statement: Every equivalence class of positive-definite ternary quadratic forms of discriminant $d$ contains a representative \[ F(x_1,x_2,x_3) = \sum_{i,j} a_{i,j} x_i x_j \quad\text{with}\quad 2 \max\{|a_{1,2}|, |a_{1,3}|\} \le a_{1,1} < 3\sqrt{d}. \]
conclusions: Every equivalence class of positive-definite ternary quadratic forms of discriminant $d$ contains a representative \[ F(x_1,x_2,x_3) = \sum_{i,j} a_{i,j} x_i x_j \quad\text{with}\quad 2 \max\{|a_{1,2}|, |a_{1,3}|\} \le a_{1,1} < 3\sqrt{d}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Each class of positive-definite ternary forms of discriminant $d$ has a form with $2\max(|a_{1,2}|,|a_{1,3}|)\le a_{1,1}<3\sqrt d$.
nodes.label: lem:ternary_lemma6

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 13
nodes.statement: Let $F$ be positive-definite with determinant $d$, and let $C$ be its coefficient matrix. Let $a_{1,1}$ be the smallest positive integer represented by $F$, so that \[ F(u_{1,1}, u_{2,1}, u_{3,1}) = a_{1,1} \] for some integers $u_{1,1},u_{2,1},u_{3,1}$. Replacing the vector by a primitive one if necessary, we may assume the three integers are coprime. By Lemma~\ref{constr:mkSL3_from_coprime_int} choose $U \in SL_3(\mathbb{Z})$ whose first column is this vector, and set \[ B = U^T C U. \] Then $F$ is equivalent to $F_B$, and $b_{1,1} = a_{1,1}$ is still minimal. Lemma~\ref{lem:ternary_posdef_iff} then implies the decomposition \[ a_{1,1} F_B(x_1,x_2,x_3) = (b_{1,1} x_1 + b_{1,2}x_2 + b_{1,3}x_3)^2 + G_B(x_2,x_3), \] with $G_B$ positive-definite. By adjusting $x_1$ via integer translations one arranges \[ |b_{1,2}|,\ |b_{1,3}| \le \frac{a_{1,1}}{2}. \] The discriminant condition then gives \[ a_{1,1}^2 \le 9 d, \] i.e. $a_{1,1} < 3\sqrt{d}$, completing the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Move the minimal represented value to $b_{1,1}$ by an $SL_3$ completion, decompose via $G_B$, and translate $x_1$ to shrink $b_{1,2},b_{1,3}$.

nodes.name: Minimal represented value
nodes.statement: Let $F$ be positive-definite with determinant $d$, and let $C$ be its coefficient matrix. Let $a_{1,1}$ be the smallest positive integer represented by $F$, so that \[ F(u_{1,1}, u_{2,1}, u_{3,1}) = a_{1,1} \] for some integers $u_{1,1},u_{2,1},u_{3,1}$. Replacing the vector by a primitive one if necessary, we may assume the three integers are coprime.
nodes.statement_short: Let $a_{1,1}$ be the least positive value of $F$, attained at a primitive vector.

nodes.name: Complete to $SL_3$
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{constr:mkSL3_from_coprime_int} choose $U \in SL_3(\mathbb{Z})$ whose first column is this vector, and set \[ B = U^T C U. \] Then $F$ is equivalent to $F_B$, and $b_{1,1} = a_{1,1}$ is still minimal.
nodes.statement_short: Complete the vector to $U\in SL_3(\mathbb{Z})$ and pass to $B=U^TCU$.

nodes.name: Decompose via $G_B$
nodes.statement: Lemma~\ref{lem:ternary_posdef_iff} then implies the decomposition \[ a_{1,1} F_B(x_1,x_2,x_3) = (b_{1,1} x_1 + b_{1,2}x_2 + b_{1,3}x_3)^2 + G_B(x_2,x_3), \] with $G_B$ positive-definite.
nodes.statement_short: Write $a_{1,1}F_B$ as a square plus the positive-definite $G_B$.

nodes.name: Translate and bound
nodes.statement: By adjusting $x_1$ via integer translations one arranges \[ |b_{1,2}|,\ |b_{1,3}| \le \frac{a_{1,1}}{2}. \] The discriminant condition then gives \[ a_{1,1}^2 \le 9 d, \] i.e. $a_{1,1} < 3\sqrt{d}$, completing the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Translations make $|b_{1,2}|,|b_{1,3}|\le a_{1,1}/2$; the discriminant gives $a_{1,1}<3\sqrt d$.

nodes.name: Positive-definite ternary forms of discriminant 1
nodes.statement: Every positive–definite ternary quadratic form of discriminant $1$ is equivalent to the form \[x_1^2 + x_2^2 + x_3^2. \]
assumptions: positive–definite ternary quadratic form of discriminant $1$
conclusions: is equivalent to the form \[x_1^2 + x_2^2 + x_3^2. \]
nodes.statement_short: Every positive-definite ternary form of discriminant 1 is equivalent to $x_1^2+x_2^2+x_3^2$.
nodes.label: lem:ternary_det_eq_one

nodes.name: Sum of three squares from a quadratic residue
nodes.statement: Let $n>2$. If there exists a positive integer $d'$ such that $-d'$ is a quadratic residue modulo $d'n-1$, then $n$ can be represented as the sum of three squares.
assumptions: there exists a positive integer $d'$ such that $-d'$ is a quadratic residue modulo $d'n-1$
conclusions: $n$ can be represented as the sum of three squares
nodes.label: lem:three-squares-dprime

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 15
nodes.statement: If $-d'$ is a quadratic residue modulo $d'n-1$, then there exist integers $a_{1,2}$ and $a_{2,2}$ such that \[ a_{2,2}^{\,2} + d' = a_{1,1}(d'n-1), \] for some integer $a_{1,1}>0$. Set \[ d' = a_{1,1}a_{2,2} - a_{1,2}^{\,2}. \] We choose $a_{2,2}=d'n-1$, so that $a_{2,2}>2d'-1>1$ and hence $a_{1,1}>1$. Consider the symmetric matrix \[ A = \begin{pmatrix} a_{1,1} & a_{1,2} & 1 \\ a_{1,2} & a_{2,2} & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & n \end{pmatrix}. \] Its determinant is \[ \det(A) = (a_{1,1}a_{2,2} - a_{1,2}^{\,2})n - a_{2,2} = d'n - (d'n-1) = 1, \] so the corresponding ternary quadratic form $F_A$ has discriminant~$1$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:ternary_posdef_iff}, $F_A$ is positive–definite, and by construction \[ F_A(0,0,1) = n, \] so $F_A$ represents $n$. By Theorem~\ref{lem:ternary_det_eq_one}, every positive–definite ternary quadratic form of discriminant~$1$ is equivalent to the form $x_1^2 + x_2^2 + x_3^2$, and equivalent forms represent the same integers. Hence $n$ is a sum of three squares.
nodes.statement_short: Build an explicit positive-definite ternary form of discriminant 1 representing $n$ and apply Lemma 14.

nodes.name: Quadratic residue gives coefficients
nodes.statement: If $-d'$ is a quadratic residue modulo $d'n-1$, then there exist integers $a_{1,2}$ and $a_{2,2}$ such that \[ a_{2,2}^{\,2} + d' = a_{1,1}(d'n-1), \] for some integer $a_{1,1}>0$.
nodes.statement_short: Translate the residue condition into $a_{2,2}^2+d'=a_{1,1}(d'n-1)$.

nodes.name: The ternary matrix
nodes.statement: Consider the symmetric matrix \[ A = \begin{pmatrix} a_{1,1} & a_{1,2} & 1 \\ a_{1,2} & a_{2,2} & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & n \end{pmatrix}. \] Its determinant is \[ \det(A) = (a_{1,1}a_{2,2} - a_{1,2}^{\,2})n - a_{2,2} = d'n - (d'n-1) = 1, \] so the corresponding ternary quadratic form $F_A$ has discriminant~$1$.
nodes.statement_short: Define the $3\times3$ matrix $A$ and check $\det A=1$.

nodes.name: Positive-definite and represents $n$
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lem:ternary_posdef_iff}, $F_A$ is positive–definite, and by construction \[ F_A(0,0,1) = n, \] so $F_A$ represents $n$.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 11 gives positive-definiteness; $F_A(0,0,1)=n$.

nodes.name: Conclude via Lemma 14
nodes.statement: By Theorem~\ref{lem:ternary_det_eq_one}, every positive–definite ternary quadratic form of discriminant~$1$ is equivalent to the form $x_1^2 + x_2^2 + x_3^2$, and equivalent forms represent the same integers. Hence $n$ is a sum of three squares.
nodes.statement_short: $F_A$ is equivalent to $x_1^2+x_2^2+x_3^2$, which represents the same integers.

nodes.name: Integers $n\equiv 2 \pmod 4$ are sums of three squares
nodes.statement: If $n$ is a positive integer and $n\equiv 2 \pmod 4$, then $n$ can be represented as the sum of three squares.
conclusions: $n$ can be represented as the sum of three squares
nodes.label: lem:n2mod4

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 16
nodes.statement: Since $(4n,n-1)=1$, it follows from Dirichlet's theorem on primes in arithmetic progressions that the progression \[ \{4nj+n-1 : j=1,2,\dots\} \] contains infinitely many primes. Choose $j>1$ such that \[ p = 4nj + n - 1 = (4j+1)n - 1 \] is prime, and let $d' = 4j+1$. Since $n\equiv 2\pmod 4$, we have \[ p = d'n - 1 \equiv -1 \pmod 4. \] By Lemma~\ref{lem:three-squares-dprime}, it suffices to show that $-d'$ is a quadratic residue modulo $p$. Write \[ d' = \prod_i q_i^{k_i}, \] where the $q_i$ are distinct primes dividing $d'$. Then \[ p = d'n - 1 \equiv -1 \pmod{q_i} \] for all $i$, and hence $(p,q_i)=1$ for each $i$. Therefore \[ \left(\frac{-d'}{p}\right) = \prod_i \left(\frac{-q_i}{p}\right)^{k_i} = \prod_i \left(\frac{-1}{p}\right)^{k_i} \left(\frac{q_i}{p}\right)^{k_i}. \] Since $p\equiv 1\pmod 4$, we have $\left(\frac{-1}{p}\right)=1$, and by quadratic reciprocity, \[ \left(\frac{q_i}{p}\right) = \left(\frac{p}{q_i}\right) = \left(\frac{-1}{q_i}\right) \] because $p\equiv -1\pmod{q_i}$. Thus \[ \left(\frac{-d'}{p}\right) = \prod_i \left(\frac{-1}{q_i}\right)^{k_i} = 1, \] so $-d'$ is a quadratic residue modulo $p$ as required. Lemma \ref{lem:three-squares-dprime} then gives that $n$ is a sum of three squares.
nodes.statement_short: Dirichlet gives a prime $p=(4j+1)n-1$; quadratic reciprocity shows $-d'$ is a residue mod $p$, then Lemma 15.

nodes.name: Dirichlet prime
nodes.statement: Since $(4n,n-1)=1$, it follows from Dirichlet's theorem on primes in arithmetic progressions that the progression \[ \{4nj+n-1 : j=1,2,\dots\} \] contains infinitely many primes. Choose $j>1$ such that \[ p = 4nj + n - 1 = (4j+1)n - 1 \] is prime, and let $d' = 4j+1$. Since $n\equiv 2\pmod 4$, we have \[ p = d'n - 1 \equiv -1 \pmod 4. \]
nodes.statement_short: Dirichlet's theorem gives a prime $p=d'n-1$ with $d'=4j+1$.

nodes.name: Reduce to residue
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lem:three-squares-dprime}, it suffices to show that $-d'$ is a quadratic residue modulo $p$.
nodes.statement_short: By Lemma 15 it suffices that $-d'$ is a residue mod $p$.

nodes.name: Factor $d'$
nodes.statement: Write \[ d' = \prod_i q_i^{k_i}, \] where the $q_i$ are distinct primes dividing $d'$. Then \[ p = d'n - 1 \equiv -1 \pmod{q_i} \] for all $i$, and hence $(p,q_i)=1$ for each $i$. Therefore \[ \left(\frac{-d'}{p}\right) = \prod_i \left(\frac{-q_i}{p}\right)^{k_i} = \prod_i \left(\frac{-1}{p}\right)^{k_i} \left(\frac{q_i}{p}\right)^{k_i}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Factor $d'$ and expand the Legendre symbol multiplicatively.

nodes.name: Quadratic reciprocity
nodes.statement: Since $p\equiv 1\pmod 4$, we have $\left(\frac{-1}{p}\right)=1$, and by quadratic reciprocity, \[ \left(\frac{q_i}{p}\right) = \left(\frac{p}{q_i}\right) = \left(\frac{-1}{q_i}\right) \] because $p\equiv -1\pmod{q_i}$. Thus \[ \left(\frac{-d'}{p}\right) = \prod_i \left(\frac{-1}{q_i}\right)^{k_i} = 1, \] so $-d'$ is a quadratic residue modulo $p$ as required. Lemma \ref{lem:three-squares-dprime} then gives that $n$ is a sum of three squares.
nodes.statement_short: Quadratic reciprocity gives $(-d'/p)=1$; conclude by Lemma 15.

nodes.name: Integers $n\equiv 1,3,5 \pmod 8$ are sums of three squares
nodes.statement: If $n$ is a positive integer such that $n\equiv 1,3,$ or $5 \pmod 8$, then $n$ can be represented as the sum of three squares.
conclusions: $n$ can be represented as the sum of three squares
nodes.label: lem:n135mod8

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 17
nodes.statement: Clearly $1$ is a sum of three nonnegative squares. Let $n>2$. Define \[ c = \begin{cases} 3, &\text{if } n \equiv 1 \pmod 8,\\ 1, &\text{if } n \equiv 3 \pmod 8,\\ 3, &\text{if } n \equiv 5 \pmod 8. \end{cases} \] If $n\equiv 1$ or $3 \pmod 8$, then \[ \frac{cn-1}{2} \equiv 1 \pmod 2 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \frac{cn-1}{2} \equiv 1 \pmod 4. \] If $n\equiv 5 \pmod 8$, then \[ \frac{cn-1}{2} \equiv 3 \pmod 4. \] In all three cases, $(4n, \tfrac{cn-1}{2}) = 1$. By Dirichlet's theorem, there exists a prime number $p$ of the form \[ p = 4nj + \frac{cn-1}{2} \] for some positive integer $j$. Let \[ d' = 8j + c. \] Then \[ 2p = (8j + c)n - 1 = d'n - 1. \] By Lemma~\ref{lem:three-squares-dprime}, it suffices to prove that $-d'$ is a quadratic residue modulo $2p$. If $-d'$ is a quadratic residue modulo $p$, then there exists an integer $x_0$ such that \[ x_0^{2} + d' \equiv 0 \pmod p. \] Let $x=x_0$ if $x_0$ is odd, and $x=x_0+p$ if $x_0$ is even. Then $x$ is odd and \[ x^{2} + d' \equiv 0 \pmod p, \qquad x^{2} + d' \equiv 0 \pmod 2, \] so $x^{2} + d' \equiv 0 \pmod{2p}$. Hence it is enough to prove that $-d'$ is a quadratic residue modulo $p$. Factor \[ d' = \prod_i q_i^{k_i} \] as a product of powers of distinct odd primes $q_i$. Since \[ 2p \equiv -1 \pmod{d'}, \] we have \[ 2p \equiv -1 \pmod{q_i} \quad\text{and}\quad (p,q_i)=1 \] for every prime $q_i$ dividing $d'$. We now consider two cases. If $n\equiv 1$ or $3\pmod 8$, then $p\equiv 1\pmod 4$ and \[ \left(\frac{-d'}{p}\right) = \prod_i \left(\frac{-q_i}{p}\right)^{k_i} = \prod_i \left(\frac{-1}{p}\right)^{k_i} \left(\frac{q_i}{p}\right)^{k_i} = \prod_i \left(\frac{q_i}{p}\right)^{k_i}. \] If $n\equiv 5\pmod 8$, then $p\equiv 3\pmod 4$ and $d'\equiv 3\pmod 8$. A similar calculation, together with quadratic reciprocity, again shows that \[ \left(\frac{-d'}{p}\right) = 1. \] In both cases $-d'$ is a quadratic residue modulo $p$, and hence modulo $2p=d'n-1$. Lemma~\ref{lem:three-squares-dprime} then implies that $n$ is a sum of three squares.
nodes.statement_short: Dirichlet gives a prime $p$ with $2p=d'n-1$; show $-d'$ is a residue mod $p$ (hence mod $2p$) by reciprocity, then Lemma 15.

nodes.name: Define $c$
nodes.statement: Clearly $1$ is a sum of three nonnegative squares. Let $n>2$. Define \[ c = \begin{cases} 3, &\text{if } n \equiv 1 \pmod 8,\\ 1, &\text{if } n \equiv 3 \pmod 8,\\ 3, &\text{if } n \equiv 5 \pmod 8. \end{cases} \]
nodes.statement_short: Take $n>2$ and define $c\in\{1,3\}$ by $n \bmod 8$.

nodes.name: Congruences of $(cn-1)/2$
nodes.statement: If $n\equiv 1$ or $3 \pmod 8$, then \[ \frac{cn-1}{2} \equiv 1 \pmod 2 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \frac{cn-1}{2} \equiv 1 \pmod 4. \] If $n\equiv 5 \pmod 8$, then \[ \frac{cn-1}{2} \equiv 3 \pmod 4. \] In all three cases, $(4n, \tfrac{cn-1}{2}) = 1$.
nodes.statement_short: Compute $(cn-1)/2$ modulo 4 and show it is coprime to $4n$.

nodes.name: Dirichlet prime
nodes.statement: By Dirichlet's theorem, there exists a prime number $p$ of the form \[ p = 4nj + \frac{cn-1}{2} \] for some positive integer $j$. Let \[ d' = 8j + c. \] Then \[ 2p = (8j + c)n - 1 = d'n - 1. \] By Lemma~\ref{lem:three-squares-dprime}, it suffices to prove that $-d'$ is a quadratic residue modulo $2p$.
nodes.statement_short: Dirichlet gives a prime $p$ with $2p=d'n-1$; by Lemma 15 it suffices that $-d'$ is a residue mod $2p$.

nodes.name: Reduce from $2p$ to $p$
nodes.statement: If $-d'$ is a quadratic residue modulo $p$, then there exists an integer $x_0$ such that \[ x_0^{2} + d' \equiv 0 \pmod p. \] Let $x=x_0$ if $x_0$ is odd, and $x=x_0+p$ if $x_0$ is even. Then $x$ is odd and \[ x^{2} + d' \equiv 0 \pmod p, \qquad x^{2} + d' \equiv 0 \pmod 2, \] so $x^{2} + d' \equiv 0 \pmod{2p}$. Hence it is enough to prove that $-d'$ is a quadratic residue modulo $p$.
nodes.statement_short: Adjust parity of a square root to lift a residue mod $p$ to mod $2p$.

nodes.name: Factor $d'$
nodes.statement: Factor \[ d' = \prod_i q_i^{k_i} \] as a product of powers of distinct odd primes $q_i$. Since \[ 2p \equiv -1 \pmod{d'}, \] we have \[ 2p \equiv -1 \pmod{q_i} \quad\text{and}\quad (p,q_i)=1 \] for every prime $q_i$ dividing $d'$. We now consider two cases.
nodes.statement_short: Factor $d'$ into odd primes coprime to $p$.

nodes.name: Case $n\equiv 1,3$
nodes.statement: If $n\equiv 1$ or $3\pmod 8$, then $p\equiv 1\pmod 4$ and \[ \left(\frac{-d'}{p}\right) = \prod_i \left(\frac{-q_i}{p}\right)^{k_i} = \prod_i \left(\frac{-1}{p}\right)^{k_i} \left(\frac{q_i}{p}\right)^{k_i} = \prod_i \left(\frac{q_i}{p}\right)^{k_i}. \]
nodes.statement_short: For $p\equiv1\pmod4$, reduce the Legendre symbol to a product over $q_i$.

nodes.name: Case $n\equiv 5$
nodes.statement: If $n\equiv 5\pmod 8$, then $p\equiv 3\pmod 4$ and $d'\equiv 3\pmod 8$. A similar calculation, together with quadratic reciprocity, again shows that \[ \left(\frac{-d'}{p}\right) = 1. \]
nodes.statement_short: For $p\equiv3\pmod4$, quadratic reciprocity again gives $(-d'/p)=1$.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: In both cases $-d'$ is a quadratic residue modulo $p$, and hence modulo $2p=d'n-1$. Lemma~\ref{lem:three-squares-dprime} then implies that $n$ is a sum of three squares.
nodes.statement_short: Residue mod $2p$, so Lemma 15 applies.

nodes.name: Gauss's three-square theorem
nodes.statement: A positive integer $N$ can be represented as the sum of three squares if and only if $N$ is not of the form \[ N = 4^{\alpha}(8k+7) \] for some integers $\alpha\ge 0$ and $k\ge 0$.
conclusions: can be represented as the sum of three squares if and only if $N$ is not of the form \[ N = 4^{\alpha}(8k+7) \] for some integers $\alpha\ge 0$ and $k\ge 0$.
equivalent_conditions: $N$ can be represented as the sum of three squares
$N$ is not of the form \[ N = 4^{\alpha}(8k+7) \] for some integers $\alpha\ge 0$ and $k\ge 0$
nodes.statement_short: $N>0$ is a sum of three squares iff $N$ is not $4^\alpha(8k+7)$.
nodes.label: thm:Gauss-three-squares

nodes.name: Proof of Gauss's three-square theorem
nodes.statement: Since \[ x^{2} \equiv 0,1,\text{ or }4 \pmod 8 \] for every integer $x$, it follows that a sum of three squares can never be congruent to $7$ modulo $8$. Suppose $4m$ is a sum of three squares. Then there exist integers $x_1,x_2,x_3$ such that \[ 4m = x_1^{2} + x_2^{2} + x_3^{2}. \] This is possible only if $x_1,x_2,x_3$ are all even, and so \[ m = \left(\frac{x_1}{2}\right)^{2} + \left(\frac{x_2}{2}\right)^{2} + \left(\frac{x_3}{2}\right)^{2}. \] Therefore $4^{\alpha}m$ is the sum of three squares if and only if $m$ is the sum of three squares. This proves that no integer of the form $4^{\alpha}(8k+7)$ can be a sum of three squares. Every positive integer $N$ can be written uniquely in the form \[ N = 4^{\alpha} m, \] where either $m\equiv 2 \pmod 4$ or $m\equiv 1,3,5,$ or $7 \pmod 8$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:n2mod4} and Lemma~\ref{lem:n135mod8}, the integer $N$ is a sum of three squares unless $m\equiv 7 \pmod 8$. This completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Necessity by squares mod 8 and descent by 4; sufficiency by writing $N=4^\alpha m$ and Lemmas 16, 17.

nodes.name: Squares mod 8
nodes.statement: Since \[ x^{2} \equiv 0,1,\text{ or }4 \pmod 8 \] for every integer $x$, it follows that a sum of three squares can never be congruent to $7$ modulo $8$.
nodes.statement_short: Squares are $0,1,4 \bmod 8$, so no sum of three is $7 \bmod 8$.

nodes.name: Descent by 4
nodes.statement: Suppose $4m$ is a sum of three squares. Then there exist integers $x_1,x_2,x_3$ such that \[ 4m = x_1^{2} + x_2^{2} + x_3^{2}. \] This is possible only if $x_1,x_2,x_3$ are all even, and so \[ m = \left(\frac{x_1}{2}\right)^{2} + \left(\frac{x_2}{2}\right)^{2} + \left(\frac{x_3}{2}\right)^{2}. \] Therefore $4^{\alpha}m$ is the sum of three squares if and only if $m$ is the sum of three squares. This proves that no integer of the form $4^{\alpha}(8k+7)$ can be a sum of three squares.
nodes.statement_short: $4m$ a sum of three squares forces all even, so the factor $4^\alpha$ can be removed.

nodes.name: Sufficiency
nodes.statement: Every positive integer $N$ can be written uniquely in the form \[ N = 4^{\alpha} m, \] where either $m\equiv 2 \pmod 4$ or $m\equiv 1,3,5,$ or $7 \pmod 8$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:n2mod4} and Lemma~\ref{lem:n135mod8}, the integer $N$ is a sum of three squares unless $m\equiv 7 \pmod 8$. This completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Write $N=4^\alpha m$ and apply Lemmas 16 and 17.
